fields.placeholder: Third lens

fields.label: Findings from C (optional)
fields.placeholder: Bullets; one per line.

fields.label: Cross-check — where do findings align/diverge?
fields.placeholder: Note convergences and tensions.

fields.label: Bias risk — which perspective dominates?
fields.placeholder: Recruitment, sampling, analyst bias…

items.name: Trigger Storming — Prompt-based brainstorming
items.definition: A brainstorming method where you use specific prompts or "triggers" – such as open-ended sentences or abstract statements – to inspire new thoughts. The triggers are designed to provoke or challenge assumptions, helping the group or individual break out of conventional ideas.
items.help: Provide your problem or topic. Optionally include some trigger prompts (one per line). The model will either use your triggers or generate its own, then explore ideas that arise from responding to each trigger.
useCases: spark discussion with provocative prompts
generate ideas from abstract or incomplete statements
boosters: Use unusual or even provocative triggers to jolt thinking in new directions.
Build on whatever associations the trigger evokes, no matter how tangential or odd they seem.

fields.label: Problem or topic
fields.placeholder: e.g., Low participation in community events

fields.label: Custom triggers (optional, one per line)
fields.placeholder:
e.g., "What if nobody had cars?"
"Imagine this problem 50 years in the future..."

items.name: TRIZ (Theory of Inventive Problem Solving)
items.definition: A method that analyzes contradictions and patterns of invention to propose principle-driven solutions toward an ideal outcome.
items.help: State the problem, list contradictions and available resources, and describe the Ideal Final Result (IFR).
useCases: resolve contradictions without trade-offs
generate inventive principles to explore
aim toward an Ideal Final Result (IFR)
boosters: Map each contradiction to candidate inventive principles.
Offer at least 3 distinct concepts referencing principles.
Briefly test each concept against constraints/resources.

fields.label: Problem statement
fields.placeholder: We need high throughput without increasing cost…
fields.description: What needs an inventive solution?

fields.label: Contradictions (one per line)
fields.placeholder:
Increase speed vs maintain accuracy…
Reduce cost vs keep reliability…
fields.description: Conflicts like speed vs quality.

fields.label: Available resources (one per line)
fields.placeholder:
Idle CPU cycles…
User-generated data…
Capacitors…
fields.description: Internal/external resources, fields, effects.

fields.label: Ideal Final Result (IFR)
fields.placeholder: Zero defects at current cost and time…
fields.description: Describe the near-perfect outcome.

fields.label: Do's (must do)
fields.placeholder: Reference named principles; give 3+ concepts.
fields.description: Positive guardrails.

fields.label: Don'ts / constraints
fields.placeholder: Avoid vague “be more efficient”.
fields.description: Limits to respect.

items.name: Value vs. Effort — 2×2 Quick Wins Matrix
items.definition: Plot backlog items on High/Low Value vs. High/Low Effort. Prioritize Quick Wins.
items.help: List items (one per line). If you have rough scores, include them like "Item | value | effort".
useCases: visualize trade-offs
identify quick wins
kill time sinks
boosters: Sort final list by “Quick Wins” first.

fields.label: Items (one per line)
fields.placeholder:
Feature A | 5 | 2
Feature B | 2 | 5
Feature C

fields.label: Scale hint (optional)
fields.placeholder: Value & Effort scale: 1 (low) – 5 (high)

fields.label: Notes (optional)
fields.placeholder: Constraints, deadlines, dependencies

items.name: Vroom–Yetton–Jago Decision Model
items.definition: A diagnostic tree to select the appropriate decision style given quality, expertise, commitment, and time constraints.
items.help: Fill the diagnostics; get a recommended style and rationale.
useCases: choose an autocratic, consultative, or group style
balance decision quality vs. speed and commitment
boosters: Answer each diagnostic question explicitly; show the path to the style.
Note risks if a faster/slower style is chosen.

fields.label: Importance of decision quality
fields.placeholder: low | medium | high

fields.label: Leader expertise on this problem
fields.placeholder: low | medium | high

fields.label: Need for team commitment
fields.placeholder: low | medium | high

fields.label: Time constraints
fields.placeholder: tight | normal

items.name: Weighted Mini-Matrix (quick score)
items.definition: Tiny decision matrix: options × criteria with 1–5 ratings; totals pick the frontrunner.
items.help: Enter options (one per line) and criteria (one per line). In “Quick ratings,” add one line per option like “Option Name: 4, 3, 5” matching criteria order.
useCases: compare up to 3 options against 2–3 criteria
force a transparent, quick pick
boosters: If a criterion matters more, duplicate it (acts as a simple weight).
Break ties with a 5-minute spike test you’ll define at the end.

fields.label: Options (≤3, one per line)
fields.placeholder:
Option A
Option B
Option C

fields.label: Criteria (2–3, one per line)
fields.placeholder:
Impact
Effort
Risk

fields.label: Quick ratings (1–5) — one line per option
fields.placeholder:
Option A: 5,2,4
Option B: 4,3,5

items.name: What If — Scenario reframing questions
items.definition: A technique of reframing problems by asking "What if...?" questions that introduce new scenarios or constraints. By imagining how the issue would look under different circumstances (e.g., different people, times, or rules), you gain fresh perspectives that can lead to innovative solutions.
items.help: Describe your problem. Optionally provide a specific "What if" scenario to explore. The model will propose its own additional "What if" questions, examine each hypothetical scenario, and then connect insights back to your actual problem.
useCases: reframe a problem by changing context or constraints
explore alternative outcomes or perspectives
boosters: Pose wild "what if" questions beyond realistic bounds to expand thinking.
After exploring an imagined scenario, extract any ideas that could be applied (even partially) to the real situation.

fields.label: Problem or topic
fields.placeholder: e.g., Difficulty in remote team collaboration

fields.label: What-if scenario (optional)
fields.placeholder: e.g., All communication had to be asynchronous

items.name: Wishing — Imagine ideal solutions
items.definition: An ideation method where you freely wish for the perfect or even impossible solutions to a problem. By articulating “magic wand” wishes without restraint, you can then work backward to figure out how to incorporate aspects of those ideal solutions into practical reality.
items.help: Describe your problem or goal. The model will generate a list of "I wish..." statements – ideal, unconstrained solutions – and then suggest ways to adapt elements of those wishes into feasible ideas or actions.
useCases: think beyond realistic constraints
identify features of an ideal outcome
boosters: Encourage even absurd or impossible wishes; they can spark real ideas.
After listing wishes, examine each to find elements you *can* actually implement.

fields.label: Problem or goal
fields.placeholder: e.g., Traffic congestion in city center

items.name: WOOP (Wish–Outcome–Obstacle–Plan)
items.definition: Wish → Outcome → Obstacle → Plan (if obstacle, then I will X).
items.help: Write a short, specific wish; name the tangible best outcome; identify the likely obstacle; define the if–then plan.
useCases: contrast desired outcome with the main obstacle
bind an if–then plan to the obstacle
boosters: Phrase the wish so it’s completable in ≤2 weeks.
Make the obstacle internal (habit/thought) when possible.

fields.label: Wish — what do I want to complete?
Obstacle — what usually gets in the way?
Plan — if obstacle, then I will…

items.name: WSJF — (Business Value + Time Criticality + Risk Reduction) ÷ Job Size
items.definition: WSJF prioritizes by Cost of Delay over Job Size. CoD ≈ Business Value + Time Criticality + Risk Reduction.
items.help: Enter relative scores (e.g., Fibonacci or 1–10).
useCases: maximize economic throughput
PI planning in SAFe
boosters: Call out assumptions; avoid gaming Job Size.

fields.label: Job / feature
fields.placeholder: e.g., Payment retries

fields.label: Notes (optional)
fields.placeholder: Dependencies, sequencing, WSJF ties

items.name: Zhongyong — Doctrine of the Mean (Confucian Moderation)
items.definition: A practical method for finding a context-appropriate middle path between harmful extremes.
items.help: List extremes, principles guiding the mean, adjustment steps, and acceptance criteria.
useCases: avoid extremes by calibrating to context
craft proportionate responses and tone
boosters: Name the two extremes explicitly, then the principled middle.
Set acceptance criteria for “balanced enough”.

items.name: Focusing — Felt-Sense Check
items.definition: A short, embodied inquiry: sense the fuzzy ‘aboutness’ of a situation and find a word/imagery handle for it. When the handle fits, a small felt shift often appears.
items.help: 1) Name the situation. 2) Sense where you feel it in the body. 3) Let a handle (word/image) come; test it. 4) Ask what it wants you to know. 5) Note any felt shift; pick one tiny, kind action.
useCases: name the ‘aboutness’ of a knotty situation without forcing clarity
move from mental fog to a small next step
check boundaries/fit when ambivalent
unblock creative work by listening to the body
boosters: Go slow. Let a vague, more-than-words feel form. Don’t force it.
Use handles (small words/metaphors) that match the feel: ‘dense’, ‘static’, ‘citrus-bright’.
Test/adjust the handle until your body says ‘yes, that’.
Wait for a felt shift (a small easing, breath, or warmth) before deciding.
Keep it present-tense and concrete; skip analysis.
items.notice: Attribution: Inspired by Eugene Gendlin’s Focusing. This is a secular, self-care adaptation; not therapy.

fields.label: Situation (one line)
fields.placeholder: What’s up, in plain words?

fields.label: Body location (where you sense it)
fields.placeholder: Chest, throat, belly, jaw…

fields.label: Handle (word or image)
fields.placeholder: ‘tight ring’, ‘static’, ‘heavy blanket’…

fields.label: Message from the felt-sense
fields.placeholder: If it could speak, it would say…

fields.label: Felt shift?
fields.placeholder: Did anything ease/soften?

fields.label: Tiny next step (≤10 min)
fields.placeholder: What kind, concrete action follows?

fields.label: Support (optional)
fields.placeholder: Water, short walk, text a friend…

fields.label: Debrief (one sentence)
fields.placeholder: What changed?

items.name: RAIN — Recognize · Allow · Investigate · Nurture
items.definition: A four-step mindfulness flow for hot emotions: Recognize what’s here, Allow it to be here, Investigate with curiosity, Nurture with care.
items.help: Prompt: “What’s here; can it be here; what’s it asking; how do I tend to it?” Keep it concrete and kind.
useCases: gentle self-inquiry when emotions spike
name what’s here without fixing
de-escalate before a hard conversation
close a loop after being triggered
boosters: Short is fine (2–10 minutes).
Use simple, kind language; avoid analysis.
During Nurture, add a physical gesture (hand to heart, softened jaw).
If overwhelmed, open eyes, feel feet, lengthen exhale.
items.notice: Attribution: RAIN is widely taught; popularized by Tara Brach. This template is a secular self-care aid; not therapy.

fields.label: Trigger/situation (one line)
fields.placeholder: What set this off?

fields.label: R — Recognize (name what’s here)
fields.placeholder: E.g., anger, shame, grief; body sensations

fields.label: A — Allow (exact phrase)
fields.placeholder: “This too belongs.” / “You’re allowed to be here.”

fields.label: I — Investigate (curious questions)
fields.placeholder: What is it asking for? What hurts? What protects?

fields.label: N — Nurture (care action/words)
fields.placeholder: Kind gesture, tone, or boundary to apply now

fields.label: Aftercare (optional)
fields.placeholder: Water, step outside, text a friend…

items.name: Parts Check-In — IFS-Inspired
items.definition: A brief inventory of inner ‘parts’ so each can be heard, reducing reactivity and increasing Self-led choice.
items.help: Prompt: “Who in me is activated, and what do they need witnessed?” No fixing; just accurate witnessing.
useCases: let different inner voices speak without judgment
unblend before deciding or replying
map protectors/exiles and what they need witnessed
boosters: Name parts with friendly handles (e.g., ‘Driver’, ‘Caretaker’, ‘Teen Me’).
Ask each part: What do you fear would happen if you didn’t do your job?
Invite Self qualities (calm, curiosity, compassion) to lead.
If blended, pause outward action until some space returns.
items.notice: Attribution: Inspired by Internal Family Systems (Richard Schwartz). This is a secular self-check, not therapy.

fields.label: Scenario (one line)
fields.placeholder: What’s happening?

fields.label: Parts present (one per line)
fields.placeholder: Name each voice briefly.

fields.label: What each part wants witnessed
fields.placeholder: Fears, needs, positive intent.

fields.label: Blending state
fields.placeholder: How fused are you right now?

fields.label: Self qualities available
fields.placeholder: Calm, curiosity, compassion, clarity…

fields.label: One Self-led step
fields.placeholder: A kind action that honors all parts.

fields.label: Boundary (if needed)
fields.placeholder: A limit that keeps everyone safe.

items.name: Noting — Mindfulness Labels
items.definition: A light mental label stream that names sensations, feelings, and thoughts as they arise, building clarity and non-reactivity.
items.help: Pick an anchor (breath/body/sounds). Label what’s present, simply and briefly. Return to anchor if swept away.
useCases: label raw experience in real time
ground during overthinking or craving
wind down before sleep
boosters: One label every 1–3 seconds. Keep it light.
Say it softly in your mind: ‘tightness’, ‘heat’, ‘worry’, ‘softening’.
If lost, note ‘lost’ or ‘thinking’, then resume.
No chasing calm; accuracy over outcome.
items.notice: Attribution: Inspired by vipassanā noting. Secular adaptation; not a substitute for medical care.

fields.placeholder: Choose one

fields.label: Starter labels (comma-separated)
fields.placeholder: tightness, warmth, tingling, worry…

fields.label: Pace
fields.placeholder: Approx. cadence

fields.placeholder: One takeaway or gratitude line

items.name: Tonglen-Lite — Breathe With Suffering
items.definition: A secular compassion breath: gently include difficulty on the inhale; offer care on the exhale.
items.help: Prompt: “Breathing in this pain as it is; breathing out relief for anyone who feels this.”
useCases: meet pain with compassion (self/others)
transform aversion into care in the moment
reset before re-engaging a hard task
boosters: Keep breath natural; don’t strain.
Use plain words: ‘Breathing in this pain as it is; breathing out relief for anyone who feels this.’
Scope can be self → one person → many; choose what’s workable.
If overwhelmed, narrow scope or pause and ground.
items.notice: Attribution: Inspired by the Tibetan Buddhist tonglen practice, adapted here in secular language.

items.name: Memento Mori — Micro-Sit
items.definition: A brief contemplation of mortality to surface what is unmistakably true right now and act accordingly.
items.help: Prompt: “If time were short, what becomes unmistakably true right now?” Then choose one tiny aligned action.
useCases: recenter priorities in 1–3 minutes
choose the one thing that actually matters today
add a gratitude/repair line before closing work
boosters: Sit upright; soften jaw; lengthen exhale.
Ask the question once, then wait.
Pick one tiny act that fits the answer.
Close by thanking someone (living or gone).
items.notice: Attribution: Inspired by memento mori reflections (Stoic and cross-cultural). Secular framing.

fields.label: Truth that appears (one sentence)
fields.placeholder: What’s unmistakably true right now?

fields.label: Tiny aligned step (≤10 min)
fields.placeholder: Concrete, reversible if possible.

fields.label: Gratitude / repair (optional)
fields.placeholder: Name a person to thank or repair with.

fields.label: Risk of neglect (name it)
fields.placeholder: What is the cost if you don’t act?

items.name: Last 2% Round — Share the Unsaid Edge
items.definition: A brief, consent-based round where each person speaks the last unsaid edge that would make the plan honest.
items.help: Prompt: “What’s the last 2% I haven’t said that would make this honest?” Name impact and a concrete request.
useCases: after alignment, surface what’s still unsaid
reduce lingering risk from politeness or fear
avoid surprises by naming edge concerns
boosters: Timebox to 1–2 minutes per person.
Speak from ‘I’, own impact; avoid diagnoses.
Name the risk of not saying it.
End with a clear request or next step.
Opt-out is allowed; consent first.
items.notice: This is a communication practice, not therapy. Use consent and timeboxes in sensitive settings.

fields.placeholder: What are we aligning on?

fields.label: My last 2% (one or two sentences)
fields.placeholder: Say the unsaid edge plainly.

fields.label: Opt-out phrase (optional)

items.name: AAR — Feelings First
items.definition: An After-Action Review that begins with where it landed in the body and what need surfaced, then moves to facts and improvements.
items.help: Prompt: “Before facts: where did this land in your body, and what need surfaced?” Then run a tight AAR.
useCases: debrief with body truth before facts
reduce defensiveness and speed up learning
surface needs that data alone misses
boosters: 60–120 seconds body truth per person before facts.
Use concrete sensations (tightness, heat, shaky).
Name the need that surfaced (stability, clarity, care).
Only then list facts, wins, breaks, next step.
items.notice: Adapted AAR structure for psychological safety. Keep it concise; not therapy.

fields.label: Sensations (raw words)
fields.placeholder: Tightness, heat, jittery, softening…

items.name: Pre-Mortem + Pre-Grief
items.definition: A planning ritual that imagines failure, names who gets hurt, and installs safeguards and exit ramps before starting.
items.help: Prompt: “If this failed, who would be hurt and what would we wish we’d said now?”
useCases: imagine failure to reveal risks and safeguards
name the human cost early
write clear stop conditions and exit ramps
boosters: Describe a vivid failure headline first.
List who would be hurt and how (humans first).
Add safeguards and early warning signals.
Write exact stop/exit conditions now.
Close with one reversible experiment.
items.notice: Ethics-forward planning aid; not legal advice.

items.name: Working Out Loud — Truth Edition
items.definition: A lightweight status pattern that names what you know, don’t know, and fear to admit—so the right help can land fast.
items.help: Prompt: “Here’s what I know, don’t know, and am afraid to admit publicly.”
useCases: real-time sharing of knowns/unknowns
reduce posturing; speed clarity
invite help with specific asks
boosters: Keep sections short; use bullets.
State what you fear to admit, kindly and concretely.
End with a precise help request and owner.
Prefer a working doc or thread for follow-ups.

fields.placeholder: e.g., Team A in #design-review

items.name: Goals of Care — What Matters Most

items.name: Competing Values Framework - Culture map to align ways of working with mission
items.definition: A culture model with four quadrants that often trade off. Clan Collaborate focuses on cohesion and participation. Adhocracy Create focuses on innovation and adaptability. items.name: Community Capitals Framework - Seven capitals lens for purpose and investment

items.name: Cultural Probes & Diary Studies - Longitudinal, participant-led voice capture

items.name: Opportunity Solution Tree - Tie problems to outcomes to keep purpose tight
items.definition: A visual way to connect one outcome to the opportunities that block it, then to solution ideas and experiments. Popularized by Teresa Torres for continuous discovery.

items.name: RACI or DRCI - Clarify roles without muting voice
items.definition: A lightweight role and decision map. RACI means Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed. DRCI is Decider, Responsible, Consulted, Informed. This version adds consent gates and speak up rights so clarity does not come at the cost of voice.

items.name: Wardley Mapping - Map capabilities and evolution to protect community advantage
items.definition: Wardley Mapping is a way to make strategy visible. It begins with user needs and a value chain, then places components on an evolution axis from Genesis to Custom Built to Product to Commodity or Utility. With climate patterns, doctrine, and gameplay, you choose moves that improve position and protect community advantage.

items.name: Backcasting - Start from the desired future state and plan backwards
items.definition: Backcasting begins by describing a concrete future state at a specific date. You then work backward to identify milestones, preconditions, and actions that make the future feasible. It aligns purpose, policy, and practice without locking into premature solutions.
items.help: Fill ethics, boundary, and the future snapshot first. Add success signals, guardrails, and assumptions. Backcast milestones in reverse order, name preconditions, enablers, blockers, and no regret moves. Convert to experiments with owners, dates, and measures. Keep a simple review cadence.

items.name: PDSA — Plan · Do · Study · Act
items.definition: PDSA is a rapid-learning improvement cycle: Plan a small test with explicit predictions and measures; Do the test and gather data; Study the results against predictions; Act by adopting, adapting, or abandoning and planning the next cycle. Unlike PDCA’s pass/fail ‘Check,’ PDSA centers quantitative and qualitative learning to adjust the next test.
items.help: Use this when you want to test a change on a small scale. Fill Plan with a clear aim, change idea(s), explicit predictions, and a handful of measures with operational definitions. Keep Do to factual notes and data. In Study, compare results to predictions and note what you learned (including surprises). In Act, decide Adopt/Adapt/Abandon and plan the next cycle.
useCases: run a tiny test of change before scaling up
replace big bets with quick, low-risk experiments
validate a hypothesis with explicit predictions
improve a service or workflow week by week
collect just-enough data to learn and act
decide to adopt, adapt, or abandon a change idea
clinical QI, service design, ops tweaks, product experiments
turn complaints into measurable improvements
standardize a successful change
planning my week
boosters: Write explicit predictions in Plan; compare them verbatim in Study.
Define 2–4 measures max: at least one Outcome, one Process, and a Balancing measure.
State operational definitions: how each measure is computed (units, inclusion/exclusion).
Keep the first cycle scope tiny (one shift/day/team of 3–5) to learn fast.
Timebox the cycle (e.g., 1–7 days) and set exit criteria up front.
Use a quick run chart or before/after comparison; annotate notable events.
Capture surprises and unintended effects explicitly (good or bad).
Close the loop: Act must select Adopt/Adapt/Abandon with rationale and next-cycle plan.
Number your cycles (PDSA #1, #2…) and link each to a single aim.
If harm risk > low, insert a safety check or ethics review in Plan and Do.

items.name: Pre-mortem — Imagine Failure, Find Causes, Build Safeguards
items.definition: A pre-mortem is a prospective hindsight exercise: you assume it’s the future and the plan has failed. You list plausible causes, cluster and score them, then design safeguards and contingencies. The aim is not pessimism; it’s disciplined imagination to reduce avoidable failure.
items.help: Use this template before launch or at major milestones. Start by writing a future ‘failure headline’ and story. Brainstorm causes, cluster them, and score by Likelihood and Impact. Select the top risks; for each, define early signals and APDR safeguards (Avoid, Prevent, Detect, Respond), with owners and dates. Finish with kill/hold criteria and a review cadence.
useCases: stress-test a plan before committing resources
surface hidden assumptions and single points of failure
prioritize risks by likelihood and impact
convert top risks into concrete safeguards and playbooks
set kill/hold criteria and early-warning signals
align a diverse group around ‘how this could fail’ safely
boosters: Timebox to 45–60 minutes; smaller first. Psychological safety first: ‘Blame the plan, not the people.’
Start with a vivid ‘failure headline’ dated in the future to unlock concrete thinking.
Silent brainstorm → round-robin share → then cluster; this prevents loud-voice bias.
Score risks with a simple 1–5 Likelihood × 1–5 Impact to focus the room.
Design safeguards in four layers: Avoid, Prevent, Detect, Respond (APDR).
Define early-warning signals and tripwires with named owners.
Write pre-commitment rules: kill/hold criteria that auto-trigger review.
End with one page: Top risks, APDR safeguards, owners, dates, review cadence.
Schedule a mid-course ‘pre-mortem check-in’ now; treat it as non-negotiable.

items.name: Personal Kanban + WIP Limits — Backlog → Doing (limit 1–3) → Done
items.definition: Personal Kanban is a pull-based workflow with two rules: visualize your work and limit your work-in-progress (WIP). You maintain a Backlog, pull a tiny number (1–3) into Doing, and move finished items to Done. WIP limits create focus, reveal bottlenecks, and increase throughput without heavy tooling.
items.help: Start by listing everything in Backlog. Choose at most 1–3 items for Doing (your WIP cap). Optionally stage 3–5 in Ready/Next. If something blocks, move it to Blocked and write an explicit unblock step. Finish before you pull. Review daily and weekly; adjust WIP caps to match your real capacity.
useCases: turn a pile of to-dos into a pull-based, visual flow
stop multitasking by limiting work-in-progress (WIP)
plan your day/week with a simple board
finish more by starting less; reduce thrash and context switching
surface blockers early and make them actionable
create a gentle cadence for weekly planning and daily focus
boosters: Set a hard WIP cap for Doing (start at 1–3). If you’re over the cap, you must finish or move something out before pulling new work.
Add a small ‘Ready/Next’ buffer (WIP 3–5) so Backlog stays long-term and calm.
Use ‘Blocked’ as a spotlight, not a parking lot. Every blocked item gets an unblock action and a named owner.
Time-block your Doing items: put them on a calendar to defend focus windows.
Add ‘Aging WIP’ markers: if an item sits >2 days in Doing, force a decision (split, unblock, or drop).
Define ‘Done-Done’: finished, checked, and logged—no loose ends.
Use Classes of Service: Standard, Fixed-Date (deadline), Expedite (limit 1), Intangible (maintenance).
End each day with a 5-minute flow check; end each week with a 15-minute retro.
Prefer splitting over stretching: if a Doing task won’t fit in one focus block, split it.

items.name: Decision Matrix (Weighted) — Compare by Criteria, Not Vibes
items.definition: A weighted decision matrix compares options against shared criteria. Each criterion has a weight that reflects importance and a polarity (benefit: higher is better; cost: lower is better). Options are rated on a defined scale (e.g., 1–5). Ratings are normalized and multiplied by weights to produce a comparable total score.
items.help: 1) List options. 2) Define 3–7 criteria with weights that sum ~100% and mark each as benefit or cost. 3) Choose a rating scale (min/max) and anchor examples. 4) Rate each option on each criterion. 5) The matrix normalizes scores and applies weights; highest total wins (subject to must-haves). 6) Do a quick sensitivity check and write the decision rule and next steps.
useCases: choose among tools, vendors, roles, or project options with clarity
make a hiring or purchasing decision with explicit trade-offs
rank travel plans, courses, or design alternatives
align a group on what matters (criteria + weights) before picking
stress-test a ‘favorite’ option against shared criteria
boosters: Separate *what matters* (criteria + weights) from *how options score*. Lock the weights first.
Use both benefit criteria (higher is better) and cost criteria (lower is better). Name the polarity.
Keep 3–7 criteria. More than that dilutes focus and invites noise.
Define the rating scale (e.g., 1–5). Give anchor examples for 1, 3, 5 to reduce rater drift.
Normalize weights (sum to 100%). If not exact, auto-normalize—just say so.
Add at least one balancing criterion (e.g., risk, effort, equity impact) to avoid tunnel vision.
Run a quick sensitivity check: nudge a single weight ±10% and see if the winner changes.
Record must-haves (hard constraints) *before* scoring so you don’t bend the rules later.
Invite a devil’s advocate to score independently; compare deltas where you diverge.

items.name: Checklists (Gawande-style) — Turn Recurring Tasks into Zero-Brain-Power Steps
items.definition: A Gawande-style checklist is a short, plain-language list of the critical steps placed at a pause point. It is designed to be read and used in real time—either as Do-Confirm (work first, then confirm) or Read-Do (read an item, then do it). It focuses on preventing frequent, serious, or easy-to-miss failures and making teamwork explicit.
items.help: 1) Define the pause point and checklist type. 2) Draft the critical few items in imperative verbs; mark killer items with `!` or `★`. 3) Add call-and-response for high-risk steps. 4) Keep ≤9 items per section; split if needed. 5) Simulate, trim, and format for one page. 6) Version it, set review dates, and track adoption.
useCases: standardize recurring procedures so they’re done the same safe way every time
compress complex work into a short list of the critical few steps
make team coordination explicit (names, roles, call-and-response checks)
reduce errors under time pressure or distraction
onboard new teammates fast with a single, printable source of truth
create personal daily/weekly checklists that actually get used
boosters: Choose the checklist type first: **Do-Confirm** (do work from memory, then confirm) or **Read-Do** (read each step, then do it). Hybrid is fine.
Place the checklist at a **pause point** (e.g., before/during/after a critical phase).
Limit to the **critical few** (5–9 items per section). If it doesn’t prevent a common failure, cut it.
Use **plain, imperative verbs** (“Verify ID,” “Start timer,” “Label sample”). Avoid paragraphs.
Mark **killer items** (the truly can’t-miss steps). Use a clear marker like `!` or `★`.
Add **call-and-response** for high-risk steps (reader calls item; doer confirms aloud).
Timebox to **≤60–90 seconds** per section. If longer, split into another pause point.
Make it **single-page, high-contrast, ≥12–14pt**, big checkboxes, and enough white space.
Include a **team brief** line (names/roles/concerns) when coordination matters.
Test with a quick **table-top simulation**; revise ruthlessly; version and review on a cadence.

items.name: SBAR for Health — Situation · Background · Assessment · Recommendation (+ Provisional/Differential/Working Dx)
items.definition: SBAR is a structured handoff and communication tool (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) used by clinicians to transmit critical information quickly. In this version, you’ll also record a provisional diagnosis, a differential diagnosis (alternative explanations), and a working diagnosis (the current best explanation to test). The aim is a clear, brief message for your clinician—no jargon required from you, just the facts in order—while the generated output uses clinical language suitable for MD/DO teams.
items.help: Use this before calling or visiting your clinician. Fill in plain language—what’s happening now, what led up to it, your notes, and what you hope to get today. The output will format a professional SBAR-style summary with added provisional/differential/working diagnoses for clinical clarity. This is not medical advice; in an emergency, call local emergency services.
useCases: prepare for a doctor’s visit, urgent care, or nurse triage call
summarize your story clearly so clinicians can act fast
organize symptoms, timing, and day-to-day impact
capture your best-guess (provisional) and alternatives (differential)
set clear goals for today’s visit and next steps
boosters: Construct a concise **problem representation** using **semantic qualifiers** (acute vs. subacute vs. chronic; focal vs. diffuse; intermittent vs. persistent; progressive vs. static).

In the Assessment, draft a **provisional diagnosis** and a **tiered differential diagnosis (DDx)** using **base rates (pretest probability)** and, when relevant, **likelihood ratios** from key historical or exam findings.
Include **working diagnosis** only after integrating HPI, exam summaries, salient positives/negatives, and any available POCT/labs; make explicit **safety-net** and **return precautions**.
Perform an explicit **cognitive forcing strategy** review: screen for **anchoring**, **premature closure**, **confirmation bias**, **availability bias**, and **base-rate neglect**.

Use standardized structure for history: **HPI** (onset, chronology, modifiers), **ROS** (targeted positives/negatives), **PMH/PSH**, **FH**, **SH** (tobacco, alcohol, substances; housing; occupational), **Meds/All** (reconcile doses/PRN/OTC/supplements).

Quantify severity (e.g., **VAS/NRS pain scales**), and include **functional status** (ADLs/IADLs), **psychological state** (mood, anxiety, sleep), and **risk factors** (e.g., VTE, metabolic, obstetric).
When appropriate, reference **validated clinical decision rules** (e.g., Wells, PERC, Ottawa, Centor/McIsaac) and identify what data is missing to apply them.
Formulate **Recommendations** as **shared decision** options with **benefit–harm tradeoffs**, **test thresholds**, **treatment thresholds**, and contingency plans.
For mental health concerns, add a **brief cognitive/affective appraisal** (triggers, appraisals, behaviors, safety) and screen signal (e.g., PHQ-2/9 items requested) without self-diagnosing.

Document **red flags** explicitly (e.g., rapidly progressive neuro deficit, chest pain with hemodynamic compromise), but avoid self-management beyond basic safety instructions; defer to clinician judgment.

items.name: SOAP Diary — Subjective · Objective · Assessment · Plan (+ Provisional/Differential/Working Dx)
items.definition: A SOAP note is a structured way to track health information: Subjective (your story), Objective (numbers and observations), Assessment (the best explanation and alternatives), and Plan (what to do next). This version adds clinician-grade structure—provisional diagnosis, differential diagnosis, and working diagnosis—using technical concepts (problem representation, semantic qualifiers, Bayesian reasoning) while keeping your data entry simple and plain-language.
items.help: Fill this out in your own words. Keep it short and honest. Bring or send the generated summary to your clinician. This helps them act faster and safer. This is not medical advice—if you think you’re in danger, call your local emergency number.
useCases: track symptoms, timing, and day-to-day impact between visits
prepare a clear summary for a doctor, urgent care, or nurse line
capture your best-guess and alternatives to discuss (not to self-diagnose)
organize numbers (temperature, blood pressure, sugar, weight, oxygen, pain) in one place
write down questions, next steps, and safety reminders
boosters: Generate a compact **problem representation** using **semantic qualifiers** (acute/subacute/chronic; intermittent/persistent; progressive/static; focal/diffuse; pleuritic/pressure-like) with **illness script** cues.

Construct a **provisional diagnosis** and a **prioritized differential diagnosis (DDx)** using **pretest probability**, **Bayesian updating**, and (where applicable) **likelihood ratios** from historical and exam findings.

Select a **working diagnosis** only after integrating **HPI**, **salient positives/negatives**, any **POCT**/**labs**, and functional status; articulate **test thresholds** vs **treatment thresholds** and specify **safety-net**/**return precautions**.
Perform a **cognitive forcing strategy** review for **anchoring**, **premature closure**, **confirmation bias**, **availability bias**, **base-rate neglect**, and **commission bias**.

For psych/behavioral health entries, add a brief **cognitive/affective appraisal** (automatic thoughts, core beliefs, behavioral responses); optionally include **PHQ-9/GAD-7** signal requests, **C-SSRS** flags if safety concerns arise, and **DSM-5 cross-cutting** symptom items as prompts.

Use standardized structure: **HPI**, targeted **ROS**, **PMH/PSH**, **FH**, **SH** (tobacco/alcohol/substances; housing; intimate partner safety; occupation), **Meds/All** (reconcile dose/route/frequency; PRN; OTC; supplements).

Consider validated decision tools when applicable (e.g., **Wells/PERC** for VTE, **Centor/McIsaac** for pharyngitis, **Ottawa** rules for minor trauma); document when data are insufficient to apply a rule.
Quantify severity with **NRS/VAS** scales; include **ADLs/IADLs** impact and **performance status**; document **red flags** (e.g., neurologic deficits, hemodynamic instability, GI bleed signs).
When uncertainty is high, explicitly record **diagnostic momentum** risks and plan **time-dependent re-evaluation** (watchful waiting vs escalation) with **shared decision**.

items.definition: Ask-Me-3 is a simple set of three questions to structure a health conversation. This template keeps your inputs plain and human while generating a clinician-style brief that layers in technical reasoning: provisional diagnosis, differential diagnosis, and a working diagnosis scaffold (the clinician’s current best explanation) with cognitive/affective appraisal and safety-netting. Goal: faster, clearer MD/DO communication without you needing medical jargon.
items.help: Answer in your own words. Bring or send the generated summary to your clinician. This organizes your story and questions; it is not medical advice. If you feel in danger or your symptoms are severe/worsening, call your local emergency number.
useCases: prep for a doctor/urgent care/nurse line conversation using Ask-Me-3
summarize in plain language, then auto-format a clinician-grade brief
capture your best-guess (provisional) and alternatives (differential) without self-diagnosing
record numbers (temperature, blood pressure, oxygen, blood sugar, weight, pain) in one place

boosters: Construct a **problem representation** with **semantic qualifiers** (acute/subacute/chronic; intermittent/persistent; progressive/static; focal/diffuse; pleuritic/pressure-like; exertional/non-exertional).

Formulate a **provisional diagnosis** and a **prioritized differential diagnosis (DDx)** anchored to **pretest probability**; when feasible, reference **likelihood ratios**, **Bayesian updating**, and **disease base rates**.

Designate a **working diagnosis** only after integration of HPI, exam, salient positives/negatives, and any **POCT/labs/imaging**; specify **test thresholds**, **treatment thresholds**, **safety-net**, and **return precautions**.

Use structured history elements: **HPI**, targeted **ROS**, **PMH/PSH**, **FH**, **SH** (tobacco/alcohol/substance, housing, occupational), **Meds/All** (full reconciliation: dose/route/frequency; PRN/OTC/supplements).

For psych presentations, include a **cognitive/affective appraisal** (automatic thoughts, core beliefs, behavioral responses), consider **PHQ-2/9** or **GAD-7** signals when indicated, and always assess safety (e.g., **C-SSRS** triggers).
When applicable, cite validated rules (e.g., **Wells/PERC** for VTE, **Centor/McIsaac** for pharyngitis, **Ottawa** rules for minor trauma) and note when data are insufficient to apply a rule.
Communicate recommendations via **shared decision**, articulating **benefit–harm tradeoffs** and **patient values/preferences**; document **teach-back** and create explicit **contingency plans**.

items.name: Teach-Back — Restate Instructions; Confirm & Correct (+ Provisional/Differential/Working Dx)
items.definition: Teach-Back is a ‘closed-loop’ way to confirm understanding: you restate the plan in your own words and the clinician corrects anything that’s off. This template keeps your typing simple while generating a clinician-style brief with technical elements—provisional and differential diagnoses, a working diagnosis scaffold, safety-netting, and cognitive/affective notes—so MD/DO teams can verify clarity and completeness fast.
items.help: Use this right after a visit or call. Write what you were told in everyday words, then your restatement. Add any corrections the clinician gave. Record how to take medicines, warning signs, tests, and follow-ups. This helps you follow the plan and helps clinicians spot misunderstandings. This is not medical advice—if you feel in danger or symptoms are severe/worsening, call your local emergency number.
useCases: after a doctor/urgent care/nurse visit, restate what you heard and get corrections
turn complex medical directions into clear, checkable steps
capture what the clinician called it, alternatives being checked, and the current working idea
write down how to take medicines, watch for warning signs, and what to do next
share a clean summary with caregivers or future clinicians
boosters: Operationalize **closed-loop communication** using a **chunk-and-check** protocol with **universal health literacy precautions**; verify **information transfer fidelity** and **readback accuracy**.

Elicit a concise **problem representation** employing **semantic qualifiers**; articulate a **provisional diagnosis** and **prioritized differential diagnosis (DDx)** anchored to **pretest probability** with optional **likelihood ratios** and **Bayesian updating**.

Specify a **working diagnosis** only after synthesizing HPI, exam, **salient positives/negatives**, and available **POCT/labs/imaging**; document **test thresholds**, **treatment thresholds**, and explicit **safety-net/return precautions**.

Apply **cognitive forcing strategies** to mitigate **anchoring**, **premature closure**, **confirmation/availability bias**, **diagnostic momentum**, and **base-rate neglect**; record residual diagnostic uncertainty.

For psych/behavioral domains, include a **cognitive/affective appraisal** (automatic thoughts, affect, behavioral contingencies); consider **PHQ-9/GAD-7** screening prompts and assess safety (e.g., **C-SSRS** triggers) when indicated.

Convert directives into **implementation intentions** and **adherence plans** (dose/route/frequency, monitoring parameters, contraindications, interactions). Document **concordance** via teach-back (patient restates; clinician calibrates).

Capture **red-flag criteria**, **escalation algorithms**, and **care navigation** details (who to call, when, how). Include **follow-up intervals** and **contingency pathways** for deterioration or non-response.

items.name: Red-Flag List — Pre-Agree Triggers & Actions (+ Provisional/Differential/Working Dx)
items.definition: A Red-Flag Plan is a safety net. You and your clinician agree on the warning signs and number thresholds that should trigger urgent action, and you write down the exact steps to take (who to call, where to go). This version keeps your entries simple and plain while generating a clinician-style, technical ‘trigger–response’ brief that layers in provisional, differential, and working diagnoses, plus safety-net reasoning and cognitive/behavioral notes.
items.help: Fill this out with your clinician’s guidance. Use everyday words. Keep it somewhere easy to grab. This organizes warning signs and actions; it’s not medical advice by itself. If you feel in danger or symptoms are severe/worsening, call your local emergency number.
useCases: agree with your clinician on clear ‘if X, then do Y’ emergency/urgent steps
write down warning signs and number thresholds you should not ignore
capture who to call, where to go, and how to get there (day or night)
document what the problem might be now and other possibilities being checked
share a simple plan with family/caregivers and keep it handy at home
boosters: Codify **safety-netting** using an explicit **trigger–response algorithm** (IF–THEN) that escalates from self-management → same-day clinic → **urgent care** → **ED/EMS activation** based on **physiologic derangement** and **time-sensitivity**.

Anchor **red-flag criteria** to organ systems and **hemodynamic instability** (airway compromise, respiratory distress, hypoxemia, hypotension, altered mentation), plus high-risk syndromes (e.g., **ACS**, **PE**, **stroke**, **sepsis**, **GI bleed**, **ectopic pregnancy**, **testicular torsion**, **status asthmaticus**, **DKA/HHS**).

Document a **problem representation** with **semantic qualifiers** and articulate **provisional diagnosis**, **prioritized differential diagnosis (DDx)** with **pretest probability**, and a **working diagnosis** contingent on further H&P/POCT/labs/imaging; note **test/treat thresholds**.

Embed **cognitive forcing strategies** to mitigate **anchoring**, **premature closure**, **confirmation/availability bias**, and **diagnostic momentum** when interpreting at-home metrics or new symptoms.

For mental/behavioral health, include **cognitive/affective appraisal** and explicit **safety pathways** for **suicidality**, **homicidality**, **psychosis**, or **withdrawal**, leveraging tools like **C-SSRS** triggers for immediate escalation.

Pre-author **care navigation**: verified **ED destination**, **urgent care** alternative, **after-hours on-call** number, **transport plan**, language/communication supports, and who accompanies the patient; ensure **closed-loop communication** via **Teach-Back**.

Record **return precautions** with objective **tripwires** (numeric thresholds, duration, pattern change) and assign **owners**; review/redocument at defined intervals to maintain **clinical fidelity**.

items.name: Shared decision (SDM) — Options → Benefits/Risks → Values/Preferences → Decide → Review (+ Provisional/Differential/Working Dx)
items.definition: Shared decision (SDM) is a structured conversation where you and your clinician choose among reasonable options by weighing benefits, risks, uncertainties, and what matters most to you. This template keeps your entries simple and plain, then generates a clinician-style brief—complete with provisional/differential/working diagnoses, risk framing (ARR/NNT), and safety-net planning—so MD/DO teams can check accuracy and document the plan.
items.help: Use everyday words. List the options you were offered (including ‘do nothing/watchful waiting’ if relevant). Write what you see as the upsides, downsides, and unknowns, plus what matters most to you. The output will format a professional SDM summary for your clinician. This is not medical advice—if you feel in danger or symptoms are severe/worsening, call your local emergency number.
useCases: prepare for a conversation where more than one reasonable medical option exists
compare options in plain language while producing a clinician-grade brief
make trade-offs clearer using your values and practical limits
capture provisional/differential/working diagnoses to anchor the decision
record the decision, consent elements, and the review plan in one place
boosters: Formulate a concise **problem representation** using **semantic qualifiers** (acute vs. chronic; focal vs. diffuse; intermittent vs. persistent; progressive vs. static) and tie it to **pretest probability** for candidate etiologies.

Explicitly state **provisional diagnosis** and a **prioritized differential diagnosis (DDx)**; acknowledge **diagnostic uncertainty** and apply **Bayesian updating** as new data arrive (POCT, labs, imaging).

When describing options, provide **absolute risks** and **absolute benefits** (ARR/ARI), **Number Needed to Treat/Harm (NNT/NNH)**, **time-to-benefit**, and **evidence quality** (e.g., GRADE). Avoid isolated **relative risk** metrics.

Integrate **patient values and preferences** with **benefit–harm tradeoffs**, **burden**, **cost/financial toxicity**, **access**, **equity**, and **caregiver context**; document **test thresholds** and **treatment thresholds**.

Perform **cognitive forcing strategy** checks for **anchoring**, **premature closure**, **framing effects**, **availability bias**, **commission bias**, and **diagnostic momentum**; use **balanced framing** (both gains and losses).

For psych/behavioral elements, add a **cognitive/affective appraisal** (automatic thoughts, affect, behaviors) and, when indicated, brief screens (e.g., **PHQ-9**, **GAD-7**) and **safety pathways** (e.g., **C-SSRS** triggers).
Use **closed-loop communication** and **Teach-Back** to verify comprehension; document **concordance** and elements of **informed consent** (indications, alternatives, risks, benefits, uncertainty).

Plan **time-contingent re-evaluation** (watchful waiting vs escalation), specify **return precautions**, and predefine **failure-of-therapy** criteria; schedule a **decision review** to mitigate post-decision **regret** and **omission bias**.

items.name: BPMH — Best Possible Medication History (+ Provisional/Differential/Working Dx)
items.definition: BPMH is a best-source medication list built by carefully checking what you actually take—prescriptions, over-the-counter items, vitamins, and supplements—plus how you take them and why. This template keeps your typing simple and plain, then generates a clinician-style reconciliation brief (with technical add-ons like provisional/differential/working diagnosis context, safety-netting, and cognitive/behavioral notes) so teams can verify and correct quickly.
items.help: Gather your pill bottles, inhalers, patches, eye/ear drops, creams, syringes/pens, and your pharmacy info. Type each item on its own line following the example. Simple words are fine. Bring or send the output to your clinician or pharmacist. This helps them check for mix-ups. This is not medical advice—if you’re in danger or feel very unwell, call your local emergency number.
useCases: keep one accurate list of all medicines, vitamins, and supplements
prepare for any clinic, ER, pharmacy, or hospital visit
share a simple list with family/caregivers and new clinicians
track who prescribed each item and why you take it

boosters: Perform a **BPMH** via multi-source triangulation: patient/caregiver interview, **brown-bag review** (physical containers), community/specialty **dispense histories**, PHR/EMR med lists, and recent **discharge summaries**; assign **source reliability** for each item.

Document each agent with **generic name**, **strength**, **dose/route/frequency (DRF)**, **indication (problem–drug pairing)**, **prescriber/service**, **start/stop dates**, **last dose time**, and **PRN contingencies**; include **OTC**, **herbals**, **nutraceuticals**, and **topicals/inhaled/injectables**.

Execute **medication reconciliation** against the active med list; identify **Medication Therapy Problems (MTPs)**: unnecessary therapy, needs additional therapy, ineffective therapy, **dose too low/high**, **adverse drug reaction**, **nonadherence**, and **drug–drug/drug–disease** interactions.

Screen for **polypharmacy** and **Potentially Inappropriate Medications (PIMs)** (e.g., **Beers Criteria**, **STOPP/START**, anticholinergic burden, **QTc-prolonging** agents, **renal/hepatic** dose adjustments, **high-alert** meds: insulin, anticoagulants, opioids, antiarrhythmics, lithium, clozapine, digoxin).
Record **allergies vs intolerances** with **reaction phenotype** (e.g., IgE-mediated anaphylaxis vs side effect) and **severity**; add **desensitization** status if relevant.

Elicit **adherence** using neutral questions (**Morisky-like** prompts), **cost/access barriers**, **cognitive/affective appraisal** (beliefs about medicines), and **implementation intentions**; document **concordance** after **Teach-Back**.

Tie the BPMH to diagnostic reasoning: write a concise **problem representation** with **semantic qualifiers**; state **provisional dx**, **prioritized differential (DDx)** with **pretest probability/Bayesian** thinking, and a **working diagnosis** with **test/treat thresholds** and **safety-net**/**return precautions**.

For psychotropics, monitor **metabolic risk**, **EPS**, **lithium levels**, **clozapine ANC**, **serotonergic toxicity**; for cardiometabolic agents, track **BP/HbA1c/lipid** targets; note required **TDM**/**labs**.

Technical: operationalize problem–solution fit by decomposing functional, emotional, and social JTBD into verifiable interventions, evidence, and positioning claims.

boosters: Write in simple, honest language first; polish later.

items.name: STAR / SOAR Stories (Job Search)

boosters: Write plainly first; numbers beat adjectives.

Tag 3–5 competencies per story to match the job post.

items.name: Gartner-style Quadrant (Informal) — Execute × Vision
items.definition: An informal Magic-Quadrant-style scaffold: define axis rubrics with explicit anchors and weights, score vendors, normalize if needed, and place them on Ability to Execute (Y) × Completeness of Vision (X) with clusters and uncertainty.
items.help: Fill scope and ICP. Write 5–8 criteria for each axis as ‘Name=weight — anchors: 0…, 3…, 5…’. Paste vendors (one per line) with exec and vision scores like ‘Reliability=4’. Create segment-specific quadrants with different weights and anchors.
Show movement year-over-year and link roadmap/GTM work to axis deltas.
Cluster a market into Leaders, Challengers, Visionaries, Niche with uncertainty shown.
rank vendors against a transparent rubric before shortlisting
normalize mixed evidence into anchored 0-5 scores
apply different weights for enterprise vs mid-market ICPs
produce a plot spec with bubble size and color encodings
limit label callouts to avoid chart soup
log dated sources per vendor for auditability
enable clustering when eyeballing is weak
ship an executive one-pager that explains the quadrants
turn axis gaps into a two-quarter movement plan
compare segments by generating one plot per ICP
export a scoring scaffold for analysts to fill
include uncertainty bands or notes when evidence is thin
run a portfolio view to spot gaps and cannibalization
show year-over-year movement with sprites
align stakeholders on the rubric before procurement
boosters: Generates a scored placement table with weighted criteria, optional normalization (min–max or z-score), and cluster labeling.
Accepts written anchors for 0/3/5 per criterion to reduce score drift; echoes them in the output.
Supports uncertainty halos, bubble sizes (revenue/install base), and color facets (segment/region).
Includes a movement playbook: which 2 criteria to lift for maximal ‘up’ or ‘right’ motion next quarter.
Write 0/3/5 anchors for every criterion; if preset_rubric is tight and inputs are blank, inject defaults.
If scoring_method is z-score, emit mean and sd placeholders and show the rescale step to 0-5.
If scoring_method is min-max, emit min and max placeholders and show the rescale step to 0-5.
When clustering is not none, add a stability note and a seed sweep checklist.
Restrict label callouts to callouts_max and state how many were hidden.
If uncertainty_viz is not none, add error columns or confidence notes.
If variant is segmented, generate separate weight tables and plots per segment.
If variant is time-series, add a sprite table with t-1 to t deltas.
If variant is portfolio, add a block for Our products and flag overlaps.
Map bubble_size to revenue or install_base; if neither is known, default to normalized headcount.
Insert a quadrant reading guide with buyer prompts for each archetype.

items.name: 3C → STP → 4P/7P Strategy Stack
items.definition: A complete scaffold that moves from situational read (3C) to segment choice and position (STP) to a 4P/7P marketing mix with evidence and metrics.
items.help: Fill top to bottom. In 3C, be candid: strengths, constraints, unit economics, and channels you actually control. In STP, list candidate segments, then score them with a clear rubric before you pick a primary and secondaries. Write a positioning sentence using target, outcome, frame of reference, point of difference, and reasons to believe. In 4P/7P, map each P back to your proof pillars so execution cannot drift from the claim. Set practical KPIs, risks, and 90-day moves. Choose service intensity to toggle 4P vs 7P. Pick output depth to control verbosity.

items.name: Channel Teardown: Acquire, Activate, Retain
items.definition: A practical scaffold to compare how competitors acquire, activate, and retain across core channels, score what works, and convert findings into 30-day counter-moves.
items.help: Timebox to one week. List competitors and ICPs. For each channel, collect artifacts and public signals, then run a fast activation walkthrough and note retention proxies. Score channels 1–5 on Efficiency, Scale, Repeatability, and Strategic Fit with one line of evidence each. Use the CAC proxy formulas to sanity-check claims. Finish with two counter-moves, one activation patch, and a 30-day review plan. Use Outline only for facilitation, Table + labels for working docs, and Full canvas for exec-ready readouts.
useCases: Map how competitors acquire users across search, social, partners, PLG, field, and marketplaces.
Estimate activation speed and friction from signup to first value for each competitor.
Assess retention proxies such as release cadence, education cadence, and community health.
Identify observable price fences and discount patterns that affect channel performance.
Score each channel on Efficiency, Scale, Repeatability, and Strategic Fit with evidence.
Spot channel gaps and over-investments to shape counter-moves and experiments.
Compare search footprints and ad patterns on BOFU and MOFU keyword clusters.
Reverse-engineer social creative systems, creator programs, and remarketing loops.
Evaluate partner ecosystems, directories, certifications, and co-sell machinery.
Audit PLG motions for TTFV, upgrade fences, and collaboration-driven growth loops.
Analyze field sales artifacts for enterprise readiness and ABM signals.
Benchmark marketplace presence, reviews, private offers, and platform programs.
Build a comparative economics view of CAC proxies and payback by channel.
Localize the teardown by region to reflect cultural and platform differences.
Create a 30-day action plan with two highest-delta channel counter-moves.
Prioritize product or content work that unlocks channel scale or efficiency.
Set quarterly goals and re-score channels to show directional movement.
Brief executives with a one-page table and two quadrants for clarity.
Train new team members on a shared teardown process and evidence standards

items.name: Fogg Behavior Model: Motivation × Ability × Prompt
items.definition: FBM states that a target behavior happens only when Motivation, Ability, and a Prompt converge at the same moment; design by lowering ability costs, placing the right prompt, and not relying on volatile motivation.

items.name: Enumerate First, Evaluate Second
items.definition: A disciplined workflow to enumerate the full universe of entities first and only then evaluate them, using repeatable sources, a capture model, de-duplication, coverage math, ethics, and a locked taxonomy.

items.name: EAST: Make It Easy, Attractive, Social, Timely
items.definition: A practical playbook from the Behavioural Insights tradition: if you want a behavior, make it Easy, Attractive, Social, and Timely—auditing journeys and testing lever-specific changes.
items.help: Start by defining the behavior and audience. Audit the journey step by step. For each step, write concrete changes under Easy, Attractive, Social, and Timely. Prioritize Easy first (defaults, fewer steps, plain language). Add Attractive (salience, incentive clarity), Social (norms, commitments, messenger), and Timely (fresh starts, just-in-time reminders) moves. Change one lever at a time in tests. Pair EAST with a root-cause model like COM-B so you fix capability and opportunity constraints, not just messaging.
useCases: Rewrite a transactional letter or email to lift response rates.
Simplify a multi-step form or checkout to reduce abandonment.
Tune an onboarding flow with clearer defaults and just-in-time prompts.
Design a reminder schedule that hits moments of maximum receptivity.
Add ethical social-norm lines and commitments to increase follow-through.
Make CTAs visually salient and the payoff concrete on landing pages.
Create location- or cohort-specific norm messages for compliance tasks.
Pair EAST with COM-B to address root constraints before messaging.
Build an experimentation backlog that tests one lever at a time.
Localize messages while preserving lever intent and clarity.
Set an instrumentation plan for first-action rate and latency.
Produce an executive one-pager showing planned EAST changes and metrics
Turn a support ticket hotspot into an EAST redesign opportunity
Audit civic or public-health comms for defaults, norms, and timing

items.name: Nudge: Ethical Choice Architecture
items.definition: Nudge is the design of choice architecture: structure defaults, ordering, and salience to steer choices in predictable, welfare-enhancing ways while preserving an easy opt out.
items.help: Start from a specific decision (who decides what, where, when). Choose a pro-user default with a simple, reversible opt out. Make options comparable and the key information salient at the point of decision. Place the helpful action where attention already is. Test ethically for comprehension and outcomes, monitor subgroup effects, and log the rationale. Pair Nudge with COM-B for root-cause diagnosis, and use EAST and Fogg for friction removal and timing.
useCases: Set pro-user defaults for privacy, notifications, or benefits enrollment with clear opt out.
Rewrite forms and settings to reduce steps and highlight the most helpful action.
Standardize price and plan comparisons so totals, fees, and units are comparable.
Design checkout and renewal flows that surface true totals and deadlines in plain language.
Place the helpful option exactly at the decision point within product journeys.
Tune plan pickers and menus to remove irrelevant options and declutter choices.
Draft policy or civic letters that use location-specific norms ethically and show simple next steps.
Structure employer benefits enrollment with auto-enroll defaults and easy changes.
Refactor cookie and data consent banners to be privacy-friendly and reversible.
Create escalation-safe reminder schedules that avoid nag fatigue.
Run A B tests that measure comprehension and outcomes, not just click-through.
Audit for dark patterns and replace them with transparent, reversible designs.
Plan subgroup outcome checks to catch equity regressions from defaults or ordering.
Document choice architecture decisions for regulators and internal review

items.name: Prospect Theory: Reference Points, Framing, and Loss Aversion
items.definition: Prospect Theory models choices as gains or losses relative to a reference point, with diminishing sensitivity and typically steeper reactions to losses; use framing, reference management, and probability presentation to guide decisions without distorting facts.
items.help: Specify the decision and metric first. Name the reference point (status quo, expectation, goal, or peer norm). Choose a frame: gain, loss, or both. Write the same fact two ways using identical denominators and absolute numbers. If the aim is comprehension or risk literacy, show both frames side-by-side. Avoid lottery-like wording for tiny probabilities; use frequencies. Test with A B designs that hold facts constant and measure quality-of-choice, not clicks alone.
useCases: Frame prevention behaviors with gain framing to lift adherence while preserving accuracy.
Frame detection or screening invitations with carefully tested loss framing plus absolute risk tables.
Design pricing and plan pages that set helpful reference prices and avoid fear-heavy acquisition tactics.
Write retention messaging that highlights losses from switching using concrete forfeits and migration costs.
Create balanced risk disclosures that show both gain and loss frames with identical denominators.
Audit product copy for hidden reference points and reset them with trials or benchmarks.
Plan experiments where only the frame changes while keeping facts constant.
Build benefits enrollment flows that anchor on peer norms and matched reference points.
Improve financial communications by standardizing totals and frequencies to prevent probability misreads.
Localize frames to match cultural norms about risk while keeping numbers comparable.
Educate teams with a framing library: gain, loss, and dual-frame examples for common scenarios.
Report framing effects on quality-of-choice metrics, not clicks alone.
Design onboarding prompts that avoid lottery framing of tiny chances and use frequencies.
Compose public health emails that combine loss-framed subjects with balanced, absolute-number bodies
Create newsroom or science-communication briefs that pre-specify reference points and denominators
Draft compliance-safe copy that avoids misleading frames and discloses assumptions

items.name: ABT: And — But — Therefore
items.definition: ABT is a compact narrative scaffold: establish shared ground (And), introduce a tension that breaks the pattern (But), then land the decision or action (Therefore).
items.help: Pick one focus. Write the But first as a sharp delta (e.g., churn spikes at renewal). Add two short And facts your audience already accepts. Make the Therefore a real change with an owner and date. Read it aloud—keep it within one breath. Use the one-sentence ABT as the doc header, then expand each clause into a section or slide.
useCases: Craft a one-breath opening for a talk, pitch, or memo.
Write slide titles that set context and tension with a decisive turn.
Summarize research: prior work and gap, then your contribution.
Frame a product decision: goal and status, blocker, next move.
Tighten outbound emails and DMs with one concrete ask.
Reframe a roadmap item so the decision logic is obvious.
Align cross-functional teams around a single sharp problem.
Draft executive updates that show consequence and action.
Create PRD intros that compress context into a single sentence.
Structure release notes: what was true, what changed, therefore value.
Teach students concise reasoning for abstracts and essays.
Build fundraising or stakeholder narratives with clear stakes.
Convert long copy into a crisp hero and subhead pair.
Generate alternative ABTs for A/B testing different tensions
Turn the ABT into a three-slide outline for fast decks
boosters: Enforce a single And, a single But, and a decisive Therefore.
Write the But first; if it is mushy, rewrite until a skeptic could disagree.
Backfill exactly two short And facts the audience already accepts.
Make the Therefore change behavior, scope, or hypothesis—no restatements.
Read aloud: target 20–35 seconds; cut until it fits one breath.
Swap And/But/Therefore words for synonyms without losing logic (Yet/So, However/Thus).
Generate a slide-outline: one slide per clause with receipt data under each.
Offer variants for email subject, landing hero, and PRD header automatically.
Quality checks: But-test, Therefore-test, and One-breath rule appended on request.
Owner-and-date hook so the Therefore lands on a calendar.
Graceful blanks: prints guidance when clauses are missing instead of failing.
Output modes for outline, table with labels, or a full working canvas

items.name: 3-Act Structure: Setup → Confrontation → Resolution
items.definition: A classic arc for stories that need transformation: Act 1 sets context and a point of no return, Act 2 escalates through complications to a darkest moment and insight, Act 3 commits to decisive action, payoff, and a credible new normal.
items.help: Write the climax first (Act 3 decision and the metric that proves payoff). Backfill only the Act 1 context required to make that climax make sense. Design Act 2 around a midpoint reversal and a named darkest moment. Storyboard nine cards—Setup, Turn, Consequence for each act—and cut any card that does not raise stakes or change knowledge. Ensure Act 3 ends with a visible cost or tradeoff and a short coda that shows the new normal.

items.name: Problem–Solution–Payoff (PSP)
items.definition: A persuasive pattern that links a felt, evidenced Problem to a specific Solution (mechanism), then to a concrete, time-bounded Payoff.
items.help: Start by pinning one ICP and one KPI. Make the Problem undeniable with a stat plus a scene. Name the Solution by its mechanism ("We do X by Y"), not just a brand. Quantify the Payoff with baselines and a date, and add a short "life after" vignette. Close with risk relief (proof artifacts) and a single, time-bound CTA. For technical audiences, use PMEP and include the evidence source. Test ethically and measure the outcome that matters, not just clicks.

items.name: Rhetorical Situation: Exigence, Audience, Constraints
items.definition: A diagnostic and design scaffold for communication: name a fixable exigence, target the audience who can act, work with constraints, and deliver a fitting response at the right moment.
items.help: Start with the situation, not the slogan. Write a one line exigence that names the imperfection and the modification you seek. Identify the audience who both can be moved and can act, plus the legitimizers they heed. Inventory constraints such as facts, rules, values, time, channels, and credibility. Choose a purpose, genre, tone, and kairos window that fit. Draft only what the actor needs to decide or do now. Test for fit with a reasonable actor standard and remove anything that is not needed under the constraints. Use the Bitzer versus Vatz selector to decide how much you will set salience versus accept the given situation.

items.name: Stasis Theory: Conjecture, Definition, Quality, Policy
items.definition: A dispute diagnostic and agenda scaffold that locates where the hang-up is: Conjecture (facts), Definition (classification), Quality (evaluation), then Policy (action). Settle lower stases before arguing higher ones.
items.help: Start by asking participants which stasis they believe the dispute is at. Write a one-line claim for each stasis and stop at the first one that breaks. Structure the meeting in stasis order: Conjecture, then Definition, then Quality, then Policy. Match evidence to stasis: data for Conjecture, criteria or precedents for Definition, benchmarks and values for Quality, options and owners for Policy. Close each stasis with a decision record such as We agree the facts show X. Park arguments that jump ahead. Export a decision log and assign owners and dates.

Structure an incident review so facts are settled before actions are chosen.

items.name: Topoi (Common Topics) Builder
items.definition: A reusable set of common topics (topoi) that prompt systematic questions—Definition, Comparison, Degree, Relationship, Circumstances, Testimony—to generate and test proofs for and against a claim.
items.help: Write the one-line claim first. For each topos, jot answers for your claim and for the best counter-claim. Keep it quick on the first pass. Mark which answers have evidence you can actually produce. If a topic goes empty, that signals research or scope narrowing. Converge by starring the proofs that are relevant, credible, and feasible, then stitch them into a structure (ABT, PSP, 4Ps, or 3-Act). Use Stasis Theory to keep everyone at the same level of dispute.

items.name: Argument from Consequences: Pragmatic Reasoning Canvas
items.definition: A pragmatic reasoning scaffold that maps an action to its likely outcomes (benefits, costs, risks), compares against a live alternative, selects a clear decision rule, and produces a bounded recommendation with guardrails.
items.help: Describe the action precisely (who, what, when, where). List expected positive and negative outcomes and the mechanisms linking action to outcomes. Record distributional effects, time horizon, and reversibility. Choose a decision rule and threshold. Finish with a recommendation and the metrics you will monitor. Use this for action choices; do not use it to claim a fact is true because of its consequences.

items.name: Chiasmus — ABBA Lines That Snap

items.name: Nyāya Five-Part Syllogism — Pañcāvayava Inference
items.definition: An Indian logic form that presents inference in five linked steps (pañcāvayava): Pratijñā (thesis), Hetu (reason), Udāharaṇa (rule via example), Upanaya (application/mapping), Nigamana (conclusion). Think: claim → reason → rule-as-example → mapping → conclusion.

items.definition: A communication ethic and meeting scaffold that seeks hé (harmony) through lǐ (ritual) guided by rén (humaneness), protecting miànzi (face) so relationships and cooperation endure after decisions.
items.help: Fill the meeting context, roles, options, and language moves. The template outputs a respectful plan: pre-read, ritual opening, speaking sequence, synthesis path, decision log, and private follow-ups. All selects include a “None” escape.
useCases: Run a cross-cultural decision meeting that preserves dignity and speeds consensus.
Redesign stakeholder communications to protect face while surfacing risks.
Create a respectful dissent channel that prevents quiet vetoes later.
Sequence speaking order to avoid anchoring and status pressure.
Draft face-saving rejection language for proposals you cannot adopt.
Plan gifts, greetings, and seating that signal respect without excess.
Turn an adversarial update into a harmony-seeking synthesis memo.
Coach senior sponsors to synthesize after juniors have spoken first.
Integrate SCQA substance with lǐ (ritual) delivery for exec briefings.
Establish metrics for participation breadth and dissent health.
boosters: Before–During–After planner aligned to hé (harmony), lǐ (ritual), and rén (humaneness).
Speaking-order designer: junior-to-senior with senior synthesis prompts.
Face-protecting language pack with parallel, concise phrasing.
Dissent channels: anonymous form, breakout, one-on-one prompts.
Decision rule + deadline scaffolding to balance harmony with speed.
Mitigation patterns for power imbalance and timeline risk.
Ritual signals checklist: titles, seating, hosting, silence.
Companion metrics: commitment, escalation rate, breadth of voices, dissent timing.

items.name: Two-Eyed Seeing
items.definition: Two-Eyed Seeing is a commitment to learn and act with the strengths of Indigenous knowledges in one eye and the strengths of Western science in the other, bringing both into focus together through co-governance, shared methods, parallel reporting, and shared benefit.
items.help: Complete the fields to set up co-governed inquiry. The template outputs a plan with governance (OCAP/CARE), dual methods, parallel reporting lanes (Indigenous | Science | Bridge), benefit-sharing, calendars, and safeguards for pause/stop.
useCases: Design a river-health monitoring program that blends place-based indicators with sensor data.
Co-create a public-health screening initiative with a community health council.
Stand up a responsible AI review with community veto over sensitive deployments.
Publish parallel-lane reports that honor stories, protocols, and statistical results.
Draft MOUs that encode data sovereignty, benefit-sharing, and dispute resolution.
boosters: Governance checklist: partner authority, protocols, OCAP/CARE, co-authorship, benefits, dispute path.
Method design checklist: problem in both lenses, dual indicators, seasonal timelines, community hires.
Parallel reporting pattern: Indigenous lane | Science lane | Bridge lane.
Data agreements pack: storage, access, reuse, archival, withdrawal, review rights.
Decision calendar: seasonal cycles + institutional deadlines with pause points.
Success metrics: governance used, sovereignty honored, credit, action uptake, continuity.

fields.label: Partners and authorities

fields.description: List community partners, knowledge holders, and institutional leads with decision rights.

fields.label: Purpose in both lenses (two paragraphs)
fields.placeholder: e.g., (Indigenous) Restore river well-being … | (Science) Estimate dissolved oxygen trends …
fields.description: Add exactly two entries: 1) Indigenous knowledge lens; 2) Western science lens.

items.name: Indigenous Storywork (Coast Salish — Sto:lo)
items.definition: Indigenous Storywork (Coast Salish — Sto:lo) is a relational, story-led dialogue practice that centers trust, reciprocity, dignity, and careful listening. Sessions are participant-led, paced by relationship and protocol rather than a rigid script. Closely related practices such as Yarning (Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander) and Talanoa (Pacific) share this ethos: relationship is method; reciprocity and ongoing consent are non-negotiable.
items.help: Use this template to plan, run, and return a story-led dialogue. It scaffolds relationship-first preparation, culturally appropriate openings, participant-led prompts, reciprocity and give-back, ongoing consent, member checking, and community-governed data practices.
useCases: Qualitative discovery with Elders, families, and local leaders about services, products, or policies.
Community consultations that inform programs without extractive interviews.
Reflective retrospectives after incidents or pilots, paced by relationship.
Health, education, or social services dialogues where trust and dignity are paramount.
boosters: Relationship first: purpose, protocol, and roles are co-written.
Participant-led flow: prompts invite stories; silence is respected.
Reciprocity: compensation, capacity-building, and returning results are budgeted and delivered.
Care with data: consent is ongoing; governance follows community rules (OCAP/CARE or local equivalents).
Parallel planning for related practices: Yarning (session types, Welcome/Acknowledgement of Country) and Talanoa (nurturing the vā, shared hospitality).

fields.description: Name Elders, knowledge holders, local leaders, and institutional collaborators. Include decision rights.
