items.name: Intent Dump + Constraint Sweep
items.definition: A prompting technique that starts with a natural-language intent dump and then sweeps through it to extract the core objective, constraints, priorities, exclusions, and output contract before writing the final prompt.
items.help: Useful when you know what you mean but the prompt is still carrying too much raw context. Related in spirit to prompt composition and iterative refinement.
useCases: turn a messy idea into a clean prompt
convert a brain dump into a brief
extract must-haves and exclusions
separate priorities from nice-to-haves
tighten a sprawling ask before execution
clean up this raw brief
organize my context into a better prompt
turn this into a usable request
what is the actual objective here
separate constraints from background
make this prompt more focused
reduce scope before writing
boosters: Return the cleaned prompt plus a short list of must-haves, nice-to-haves, and exclusions.

fields.label: Raw intent dump
fields.placeholder: e.g., I need help turning this messy project note into a prompt that focuses on the next deliverable...
fields.description: The unsorted context, notes, or natural-language brief.

fields.label: Core objective
fields.placeholder: e.g., Produce a concise project brief for a developer
fields.description: The one job the final prompt must accomplish.

fields.label: Must-haves
fields.placeholder: e.g., Keep the budget cap; preserve the target audience; return bullets
fields.description: Non-negotiable requirements.

fields.label: Nice-to-haves
fields.placeholder: e.g., Include optional examples; suggest one follow-up question
fields.description: Useful extras that can be sacrificed if needed.

fields.label: Exclusions
fields.placeholder: e.g., Do not build the full system; skip implementation details
fields.description: What to leave out or defer.

fields.label: Output contract
fields.placeholder: e.g., Return one tightened prompt under 200 words plus three removed ambiguities
fields.description: The expected response format, length, and success test.

items.name: Trait-Stack Output Control
items.definition: A prompting technique that steers model behavior by naming desired output qualities, then reducing the stack to ranked priorities so clarity, depth, tone, and structure do not compete blindly.
items.help: Best used when a prompt has too many quality adjectives. Complements CLEAR and other prompt-composition methods by forcing priority rather than piling on style words.
useCases: prioritize clear concise structured deep output
control writing quality without rewriting the whole prompt
rank style traits before generating
avoid conflicting adjective stacks
steer tone and structure together
make this more clear but still deep
I want concise and comprehensive
help me prioritize these style traits
improve the output quality controls
tighten my style instructions
boosters: Rank the top three traits and explicitly name what can be sacrificed if tradeoffs appear.

fields.label: Task
fields.placeholder: e.g., Rewrite this email for a skeptical executive audience
fields.description: What the model must do.

fields.label: Audience
fields.placeholder: e.g., Busy leadership team
fields.description: Who the output is for.

fields.label: Desired traits
fields.placeholder: e.g., clear, concise, structured, persuasive, empathetic, direct
fields.description: All the qualities you care about before ranking them.

fields.label: Top three traits
fields.placeholder: e.g., clear; structured; direct
fields.description: The three qualities that matter most.

fields.label: Anti-traits
fields.placeholder: e.g., fluffy, vague, too academic
fields.description: What the output should avoid.

fields.label: Output format
fields.placeholder: e.g., 5 bullets and one recommendation
fields.description: The desired shape of the answer.

items.name: Multi-Axis Organizing Prompt
items.definition: A prompting framework for organizing model output across two or more explicit dimensions, so the ranking logic, tie-break rules, and display format are visible rather than implied.
items.help: Useful when a plain list is not enough. Related to prompt composition and ranking prompts, but with stronger emphasis on explicit ordering rules and sortable output.
useCases: rank options by cost then distance
sort a list by severity and probability
compare candidates across two explicit axes
organize recommendations with tie-break rules
turn a generic list into a ranked decision aid
sort these options by two factors
group and rank the output
make the sorting logic explicit
build a decision table
organize the results by priority and effort
boosters: Name the primary axis, secondary axis, filters, tie-break rule, and output shape before ranking.

fields.label: Items or domain
fields.placeholder: e.g., Weekend date ideas in Mesa
fields.description: What needs to be organized.

fields.label: Primary axis
fields.placeholder: e.g., lowest cost
fields.description: The first sorting dimension.

fields.label: Secondary axis
fields.placeholder: e.g., shortest drive time
fields.description: The second sorting dimension.

fields.label: Tie-break rule
fields.placeholder: e.g., choose the option with the broadest appeal
fields.description: How to resolve ties.

fields.label: Filters
fields.placeholder: e.g., age 21+ only; indoors preferred after sunset
fields.description: Requirements to apply before sorting.

fields.label: Output format
fields.placeholder: e.g., ranked table with rationale
fields.description: The desired display shape.

items.name: Communication Intelligence Stack
items.definition: A communication design scaffold that treats every message as a stack of decisions: intent, audience, frame, structure, evidence, style, medium, and feedback loop.
items.help: Use this before drafting or rewriting an important message. Name what the message must accomplish, who must receive it, what frame will make it meaningful, what structure fits, what evidence earns trust, what style and medium match the moment, and how success will be noticed.
useCases: plan a stakeholder message before writing it
turn raw information into a decision-ready communication
choose evidence, frame, style, medium, and ask for a specific audience
audit whether a message serves understanding, trust, action, or alignment
boosters: Work through intent, audience, frame, structure, evidence, style, medium, and feedback loop in that order.
Adapt the message to role, decision need, time pressure, and evidence appetite; do not type the person.
Treat feedback as part of the design: what should the receiver understand, do, ask, or remember?
Link to existing structure patterns such as SCQA, COSTAR, RATIO, AIDA, and Public Narrative instead of duplicating them.

fields.label: Intent
fields.placeholder: Inform, decide, act, align, repair, motivate, teach, or remember?

fields.label: Audience
fields.placeholder: Role, stakes, knowledge level, authority, anxiety, time, incentives.

fields.label: Frame
fields.placeholder: Risk, opportunity, empathy, efficiency, strategic, quality.

fields.label: Structure
fields.placeholder: Answer-first, SCQA, claim/reason/evidence/caveat/ask, story/insight/action.

fields.label: Evidence
fields.placeholder: Data, quotes, observations, screenshots, benchmarks, cases, expert source.

fields.label: Style and medium
fields.placeholder: Direct, warm, analytical, diplomatic; Slack, email, deck, memo, conversation.

fields.label: Feedback loop
fields.placeholder: What will show that the message worked?

items.name: Cialdini Influence Principles With Ethical Caveats
items.definition: An ethical-use pattern for Cialdini-style influence principles that treats persuasion cues as transparency and literacy checks, not manipulation recipes.
items.help: Use this when a message is trying to persuade. Identify which influence cues are present, whether they are truthful and relevant, what material context the audience needs, and whether the final ask preserves agency.
useCases: audit whether a persuasive message uses influence cues ethically
separate real evidence from authority, scarcity, liking, or social-proof cues
teach persuasion literacy without normalizing manipulation
boosters: Use reciprocity, scarcity, authority, consistency, liking, social proof, and unity as cues to inspect, not shortcuts to coerce.
Every influence cue should be backed by a truthful payoff, material context, and reader agency.
Flag urgency, scarcity, social proof, or authority claims that are manufactured or unverifiable.

items.name: Trust Equation for Communication
items.definition: A communication adaptation of the Trust Equation: trust rises with credibility, reliability, and appropriate intimacy, and falls when the sender appears self-oriented.
items.help: Use this when a message technically says the right thing but may not be trusted. Score the message for credibility, reliability, intimacy, and self-orientation, then rewrite the weakest factor.
useCases: diagnose why a message may not feel trustworthy
balance credibility, reliability, intimacy, and self-orientation in a stakeholder note
turn proof, follow-through, empathy, and reader benefit into a message audit
boosters: Increase credibility with accurate claims, source quality, and caveats.
Increase reliability with clear commitments, dates, and follow-through.
Increase intimacy with appropriate empathy and context awareness.
Reduce self-orientation by making the audience benefit and decision need explicit.

items.name: Hook Taxonomy and Ethical Hook Rules
items.definition: A practical taxonomy for opening messages with attention and relevance while preserving truthful payoff and reader agency.
items.help: Use this when the first line of a message is flat or manipulative. Pick the hook type, name the promised payoff, check the ethical risk, and rewrite the opening so it creates attention without misleading.
useCases: choose an opening hook for a talk, memo, post, or lesson
audit whether a hook earns its payoff
rewrite attention-grabbing copy without clickbait or fear exploitation
boosters: Use hooks to create relevance, curiosity, tension, contrast, stakes, or human specificity.
The body must pay off the hook honestly; do not create curiosity debt the message cannot repay.
Avoid fear, urgency, scarcity, or social proof unless the underlying evidence is real and material.

items.name: Hiring Manager Risk Model
items.definition: A career communication pattern for reducing perceived hiring risk with concrete evidence, role fit, collaboration signals, ownership, specificity, and defensible claims.
items.help: Use this before tailoring a resume, portfolio, or interview story. Name the hiring risk, choose the evidence that counters it, and rewrite the claim so it is specific enough to defend.
useCases: write a resume or portfolio that reduces perceived hiring risk
map claims to evidence before applying
prepare interview stories that answer risk concerns
boosters: Treat hiring as a risk decision: can they do the work, work with us, communicate, own ambiguity, and avoid exaggeration?
For every claim, add a counter-signal: concrete accomplishment, collaboration example, ownership signal, metric, or defensible caveat.
If a signal cannot be defended in interview, soften or remove it.

items.name: Small Artifact Advantage
items.definition: A proof-of-work strategy that uses small, well-framed artifacts to make a claim visible without requiring a full portfolio case study or large public launch.
items.help: Use this when a claim is true but invisible. Pick the smallest artifact that proves the point, add context and caveats, then attach it to a resume, portfolio, lesson, or public post.
useCases: create a small proof-of-work artifact for a role, pitch, lesson, or public output
turn a claim into a concrete artifact that shows judgment
choose lightweight artifacts instead of waiting for a full polished case study
boosters: Small artifacts should prove one thing clearly: judgment, synthesis, workflow design, communication, or tradeoff thinking.
Keep the artifact bounded: one page, one diagram, one captioned screenshot, one decision log, or one before/after.
Do not imply production impact if the artifact is a sample, prototype, or personal reconstruction.
